title: Gargi's two questions
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: Gargi stands up twice, and gets an answer made of nots
carry: nirguna and saguna: beyond form, and with a face
tomorrow: can twelve years of study leave you missing the one thing?
last: THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BEING.

lines: A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.
SHE STANDS UP AGAIN. TWO ARROWS.
cards: King Janaka of Videha calls a great debate and sets out a thousand cows, gold tied to their horns, for the wisest one there. The sage Yajnavalkya tells his student: drive them home. The other scholars line up to stop him.
One of them is a woman, Gargi Vachaknavi. She asks what everything is woven on, and what that is woven on, higher and higher, until he warns her: Gargi, don't ask too far. She sits down.
Later she stands up again. Like a warrior stringing a bow with two arrows, she says, I have two questions.

teach.h: NOT COARSE, NOT FINE: THE SEER.
teach.b: Her question: what is everything woven on, past, present, future, even space? Yajnavalkya answers with a list of nots.

The Imperishable is not coarse, not fine, not short, not long, without shadow, without darkness, without air, without space. And then he turns: it is never seen, but it is the seer. Never heard, but it is the hearer.
Gargi tells the room: none of you will beat him.
Now read Isha eight, and watch the same move. Sa paryagat: he has gone everywhere. Then the nots: akayam, bodiless.
Avranam, woundless. Asnaviram, without sinews. A short a at the front works like un-.
And halfway through, the turn: kavir manishi. A poet, a thinker, who set all things in order. That's the puzzle, and it holds one of Hinduism's great teachings.
God, Brahman, can be spoken of two ways.

Nirguna: without qualities, beyond every picture, so the honest words are neti neti, not this, not this. And saguna: with qualities, a poet, a friend, a face you can garland. Hindus don't have to pick one.
That's why the same Nani who says God has no form wakes Krishna with a bell every morning, bathes him and dresses him. In the reading many teachers give, the form isn't a mistake about the formless.
It's the formless, turned toward us, close enough to love.

how: Hindu teachers describe two ways of speaking of the ultimate: by what it is not (neti neti, nirguna) and by what it is (saguna, with a form to love and serve); many families who say God has no form still wake, bathe and dress a murti every morning.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: reading the Isha as a description of a human poet
reading the Isha's list of rules for a pure body
reading the Isha's own words: a portrait in nots, then a poet

games.q: Gargi, Yajnavalkya and the verse — tap the pairs.
p: asks what everything is woven on
God with a face to love

s: Yajnavalkya answers Gargi only with nots
after the nots he turns: never seen, but the seer; never heard, but the hearer.
Isha 8 paints in nots, then turns to a poet and a thinker
akayam, avranam, asnaviram, and then kavir manishi.
Hindus who say God has no form shouldn't worship a murti
nirguna and saguna sit together: beyond form, and turned toward us in a form.

games.q: a friend visiting a temple with you whispers: 'i thought hindus said god is beyond all forms. why all the statues?' what's the fairest answer?
o: god is beyond form, nirguna, and also takes form for us, saguna; hindus hold both.
the statues are the whole thing; the beyond-form talk is just philosophy.
the Isha settles it: only the formless is real, so the statues are a mistake.
games.why: Yajnavalkya's nots and Isha 8's turn to a poet say the same thing: beyond every picture, and close enough to garland.

practice: Close your eyes. Let a picture of God come up, any you've seen: a blue Krishna, a lamp, a wide sky. On each out-breath let one go: not this, not this.
Then, if you pray, open your eyes to one image or murti you love and greet it. If you don't pray, open them to one thing you love. Both moves are the practice.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, verse eight: akayam, bodiless, and then kavi, a poet. Beyond every form, and close enough to name.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: neti neti, 'not this, not this', the Brihadaranyaka's way of speaking of Brahman by what it is not.

carryVoice: The line to keep: nirguna and saguna, beyond form, and with a face. Gargi got both in one answer. Rest easy.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 8, first line (sa paryagac chukram akayam avranam asnaviram shuddham apapaviddham)
Isha Upanishad 8, second line (kavir manishi paribhuh svayambhuh; set things in order for endless years)

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.1 (Janaka's debate and the thousand cows), 3.6 (Gargi's first questions; 'don't ask too far'), 3.8 (Gargi's two questions like two arrows; the Imperishable described by nots, then 'never seen, but the seer'; Gargi: none of you will defeat him)
